query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the spray distance to 300 mm on the HVAF-i7 system will increase the deposit thickness of FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy coatings while preserving low as-sprayed oxidation and adhesion.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with a 15–45 μm feedstock, as used in previous HVAF-M3 studies.
generation.intervention: Adjust the HVAF-i7 process to operate at a reduced stand-off (spray) distance of 300 mm.
generation.conditions: Depositions performed using HVAF-i7 on substrates including internal diameters as small as 120 mm; ambient atmospheric conditions with standard protective gas administration.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased particle kinetic energy leading to improved melting and splat formation with reduced in-flight oxidation.
generation.mechanism: Shorter spray distance minimizes particle travel time in the oxidizing environment, thereby preserving particle temperature and kinetic energy; this enhances intersplat bonding and increases deposition efficiency.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in coating thickness by approximately 20–30% relative to the baseline HVAF-i7 deposition using a longer spray distance, while maintaining similar adhesion and low oxidation levels observed in the HVAF-M3 baseline.
generation.baseline: Coatings produced on HVAF-i7 with the previously used, longer spray distance that yielded acceptable quality but inadequate thickness.
generation.boundary: Excessively short spray distances (<300 mm) might lead to particle impingement issues or substrate overheating; the intervention is expected to be effective within a spray distance range of 300–350 mm.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of thickness improvement may vary with torch configuration and specific environmental conditions; thermal gradients inside small-diameter bores may also influence outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Deposit FeCoNiCrAl coatings using the HVAF-i7 torch at the reduced 300 mm spray distance and compare them to coatings produced at the previous (longer) spray distance. Evaluate coating thickness, porosity, and oxidation levels via cross-sectional SEM, XRD, and microhardness measurements.
measurements: Particle oxidation level (via XRD or EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the reduced spray distance does not yield a statistically significant increase (e.g., >15% improvement) in coating thickness, or if it compromises the adhesion or oxidation resistance compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 4 shows the difference in the properties based on the spraying distance. As the spraying distance increases, the average thickness of the coatings slightly decreases due to a stronger scattering of the particles on the longer path. An increase in the spraying distance results in an increase in coating porosity. Porosity depends on the temperature and kinetic energy of the particles []. Particles sprayed from a longer distance have a lower kinetic energy when they strike the substrate, which results in increased porosity. High temperatures and exposure to oxygen lead to the in-flight oxidation of particles; the smaller particles undergo more severe oxidation. With an increase in the spraying distance, the particles are exposed to oxygen for a longer time, which leads to an increased content of oxides (Figure 4d). As the particles oxidize with the formation of alumina, BCC solid solution loses aluminum, which is reflected in a decrease in its lattice parameter (Figure 3b). It is known [] that when Al concentration in FeCoNiCrAlMo0.5 is lower than 10%, FCC solid solution becomes preferable to BCC. The BC chemical composition (mainly ductile materials), as well as optimized spraying parameters (dense microstructure), contributes to the reduction in the forming of microcracks when applying the same indentations loads, as shown in Figure 10b. Compared to the Cr-based system, smaller microcracks were visible at the interface substrate/BC. Due to similar chemical compositions of the substrate and BC, lower internal stresses occur when the coating cools down during the spraying process. Microcracks within the BC were only observed if the indentations were placed along intersplat boundaries. A lower crack tendency is due to a smaller quantity of intersplat boundaries, which mainly depends on the spraying powder/splat size, as well as the distribution of different adhering phases [,]. The hardness decrease in the heat-treated coatings mainly related to stress relief led to the conclusion that internal stresses were present in the as-sprayed state []. As in the Cr-based system, the heat treatment promotes a metallurgical bonding between substrate and coating and strengthens the coatings cohesion, since no microcracks were visible in the heat-treated and oxidized states. papers.title: Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder.
papers.system: FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder deposited by HVOF
papers.approach: Study of spray deposition behavior with varying spray distances to examine in‐flight oxidation, porosity formation and coating thickness as a function of particle kinetic energy and residence time in the oxidizing environment.
papers.findings: Increasing the spray distance reduces particle kinetic energy and results in increased porosity and in‐flight oxidation; thicker coatings and higher microhardness were associated with shorter distances and enhanced particle velocity.
papers.mechanism: Higher particle velocity gives sufficient melting and splat formation while reducing the residence time in oxygen; conversely, longer distances allow oxidation before impact that undermines deposition efficiency.

papers.title: Comparative Study on the Thermal Performance of Cr-CrₓOᵧ and YSZ-CoNiCrAlY Coatings Exposed at 900 °C.
papers.system: Conventional MCrAlY bond coats deposited by HVOF using the M3 system
papers.approach: Examination of deposition parameters (particle velocity, spray distance) and their effect on deposition efficiency, adhesion and eventual thermally grown oxide (TGO) formation in bond coats for thermal barrier systems.
papers.findings: A slight gain in deposition efficiency was observed when higher particle velocity was achieved; additionally, nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm were identified, which yielded better adhesion and coating integrity.
papers.mechanism: Improved kinetic energy from higher particle velocity yields better melting, particle flattening and in-flight deoxidation, thus leading to a thicker and more adherent deposit.

papers.title: In-situ CrFeCoNi medium entropy alloying coating via electrospark powder deposition.
papers.system: CrFeCoNi medium-entropy alloy coatings deposited via electrospark powder deposition (ESED) on steel substrates
papers.approach: Utilizes a low-energy spark deposition approach where optimized electrical parameters promote localized melting and deposition, with feedstock powder directly participating in spark-induced melting and solidification.
papers.findings: A parameter set employing a low pulse energy produces coatings with partly melted particles and acceptable bonding, though full melting requires higher energy input.
papers.mechanism: The spark energy overcomes interparticle gaps promoting local melting and fusion; however, energy input must be sufficient to ensure complete melting for consistent coating quality.

established: Higher particle velocity and shorter spray distances (300–350 mm) yield improved deposition efficiency and coating thickness.
Feedstock particle size in the 15–45 μm range is optimal in HVAF-M3 systems but may require parameter adjustment in different torch configurations like HVAF-i7.
In-flight oxidation during spraying is critical; increased residence time in oxygen leads to more oxidation and porosity, reducing coating quality and effective thickness.

approaches_tried.approach: Using a 15–45 μm feedstock with the HVAF-M3 torch
approaches_tried.outcome: High-quality coatings with adequate thickness and minimal oxidation were obtained.

approaches_tried.approach: Applying the same feedstock and composition with the HVAF-i7 torch
approaches_tried.outcome: Acceptable coating quality was achieved but with inadequate thickness, indicating lower deposition efficiency.

mechanisms: Higher particle kinetic energy minimizes in-flight oxidation and promotes better melting and splat formation, which enhances coating thickness and adhesion.
Increased spray distances allow particles to oxidize en route, decreasing kinetic energy and deposition efficiency.
disagreements: While some studies emphasize minor feedstock size adjustments to improve spray behavior, others indicate that the critical factor is the particle velocity governed by spray distance and torch configuration.
There is debate over whether modifications should be made in feedstock characteristics versus spray parameters to address thickness limitations.
open_questions: Can the inadequate thickness observed with the HVAF-i7 torch be overcome solely by modifying spray parameters (e.g. increasing particle velocity) without changing the feedstock size distribution?
What is the optimal balance between particle kinetic energy and oxidation control for high-density, thick, adherent bond coats using different HVAF torches?
How does the deposition performance scale when coating internal diameters as small as 120 mm, where access and flow dynamics may further influence outcomes?
opportunities: Investigate the effect of optimizing spray distance and increasing particle velocity on the HVAF-i7 system while using the established 15–45 μm feedstock.
Combine improved torch parameters (e.g. reduced standoff distance or nozzle modifications) with careful control of oxygen exposure to minimize in-flight oxidation.

Carry out systematic studies comparing HVAF-M3 and HVAF-i7 under controlled conditions to determine the minimal necessary intervention for achieving both coating thickness and quality within constrained geometries (internal diameters ≥120 mm).
Explore adjustments to the deposition setup that can be directly translated to internal surfaces without compromising thermal barrier service durability.

directions.direction: Optimize spray distance to enhance particle velocity and reduce in‐flight oxidation
directions.assessment: This approach directly addresses the thickness limitation by increasing the kinetic energy of the particles. Prior evidence shows that shorter spray distances (300–350 mm) yield improved deposition efficiency and enhanced splat formation (e.g., PMC8541463::web::022 and PMC10820071::web::010). It respects the feedstock and internal geometry constraints and is a well‐understood physics-driven intervention. Feasible experimental setups can be designed to measure deposit thickness and oxidation levels, making the study highly informative.

directions.direction: Redesign the torch nozzle geometry (e.g., adopt a converging nozzle) to boost particle velocity
directions.assessment: Altering the nozzle design is aimed at increasing the particle exit velocity even at existing spray distances. This intervention leverages the established mechanism where higher particle kinetic energy reduces pre-impact oxidation and improves splat formation (supported by PMC8541463::web::022). It is directly relevant to overcoming the thickness issue and is feasible to implement in controlled experiments, although integration with constrained geometries (internal diameters down to 120 mm) needs verification.

directions.direction: Increase the carrier gas pressure to raise particle acceleration
directions.assessment: Boosting the gas pressure is a single-parameter change that can increase particle velocity, similar in effect to reducing the spray distance. The mechanism is well supported by prior studies on deposition efficiency and spray kinetics (PMC10820071::web::010, PMC8541463::web::022). This approach is feasible and respects the material and geometric constraints; however, increased gas pressure may risk altering flow uniformity and could affect coating microstructure if not optimized.

directions.direction: Introduce substrate preheating to promote better splat flattening and intersplat bonding
directions.assessment: Preheating the substrate can reduce the thermal gradient on impact, thereby improving the splat formation and fusion of particles. This intervention has been shown to enhance coating density and adhesion (as seen in related studies on plasma spraying and thermal barrier coatings). Although slightly indirect compared to altering particle velocity, it still addresses the effective build-up thickness and ameliorates oxidation effects. It is feasible and can be tested under high-temperature service conditions.
